added_failures_note: not applicable: the reviewed run is a read-only operational survey node that changes no source and no test; its manifest records baseline_suite=null and after_suite=null (confirmed in the run's classification.json manifest data), so there are no base-arm/head-arm gate logs from which to derive an added-failure count. added_failure_count set to 0 and added_failure_ids to [] on that basis.

findings.text: nakasvr23 closed SSH at the key exchange on every attempt, so the whole survey is one-server and no host inventory, resolution, store check or slice read is claimed for it. This is the run's own disclosed limit, restated here rather than raised as a defect: the run names the failure (kex_exchange_identification, three attempts), marks the server unreachable, and makes no claim for it. The residual is that half the dispatched scope (two servers named in section 6) is unmeasured.

The dispatch's 'whether a port named in site configuration accepts a TCP connection' measure has no subject: no TCP port is named anywhere in the EQDB or EDDB configuration read (transport is a socket client, SOCKET_EQDBIO, over libEQDBMSPIC.so). The run reports this plainly as a measure with no subject rather than dropping it or guessing, and the mode-restricted eqdball helpers return Permission denied to d240044 so the socket could not be exercised even were a port named (reproduced for eqdball in batch_f.log). This is the run's own disclosure, not a defect.

The sentence 'The SSH port (22) is the only transport named anywhere' is loose: port 22 is the ssh default and is not a port named in any site configuration read (the port numbers that appear in ssh config, such as the laptop-hop transport, are on the ITER client side and outside this survey). The section's conclusion is unaffected - no TCP port is named in the sources read, which is the correct and sufficient claim.

justifications.durability: The deliverable is a static HTML evidence fragment; every factual claim is recoverable from the committed fragment text plus the run's collection logs on disk, and I reproduced the load-bearing facts independently over the fragment's own read-only ssh path. The negative control is reproduced rather than asserted (getent hosts dbsvr17p returns no record). Weaknesses: the fragment cites mutable paths outside the committed tree (/home/d240034/fbequ/EFIT95.DATA, /analysis/lib/JT60SAEQDB/eqdbms.20230523/endian_info) so a future reader without the survey's ssh route depends on the fragment's quoted outputs, which it does carry (85 names verbatim, the eqdsk_read result, the header line); and the one substantive data point, the E101011 G-EQDSK, is quoted by shape only, naming no psi values, so its numbers are not independently checkable from the fragment alone. The psi/q array shape could not be re-run independently in my session because intr26-2's python/numpy modules failed to load a working numpy, though the header line (129 129) was reproduced.
justifications.evidence: Every quantitative claim in the fragment is recoverable from the committed fragment text and the run's own collection logs on disk (logs/batch_a..g.log, logs/collect_a..f.sh). I read the logs and reproduced the counts: batch_g.log carries 85 NORESV lines; batch_e.log's endian_info section carries 85 non-empty host lines; batch_d.log lists the three FAME3 paths as 'No such file or directory' and /analysis_DB as holding only EDASDB and MBDB; batch_f.log carries the E101011 header and the eqdsk_read result psi (129,129), q (129,). I then independently reproduced the load-bearing claims from my own allocation over the same read-only ssh path the run used (ssh -F ~/.ssh/config ... jt-60sa, host intr26-2, user d240044): getent hosts dbsvr17p returned no record (rc=2), reproducing the declared negative control; the three FAME3 paths returned 'No such file or directory'; endian_info has 85 non-empty lines and 85 first-field names; echoFameHost echoes dbsvr17p with fame3 and nakasvr17 commented; and the EFIT95.DATA header line reads 'SA 25-12-03 101011 4000ms09/02/17 0 129 129'. The one claim I could not re-run independently is the psi/q array shape, because intr26-2's python/numpy modules did not load a working numpy under my session (numpy C-extension import failure), the same fragility the run's own collect_f.sh worked around; the shape is verified against the run's log and the header line (129 129) I did reproduce. Deduction: the fragment is the node's own instrument for the survey. Only one equilibrium archive is reported and the psi values are not quoted, so a reader checks shapes not numbers; and the search for other archives is a bounded find (maxdepth 3-4) over /analysis, /analysis_DB and /work, so 'no other archive' is bounded rather than exhaustive. Evidence is strong and independently corroborated at the load-bearing points.
justifications.fit: The fragment parses as HTML (html.parser accepts it) and carries 23 element ids, every one beginning with the node id jtmm-jt60sa-host-survey (zero outside the prefix, no duplicates), so sibling fragments composed into one record cannot collide on an anchor. The anchor link #jtmm-jt60sa-host-survey-nc resolves to the declared-negative-control section within the fragment. The commit subjects are conventional with bodies and no trailer, and no author or AI attribution appears in either commit or in the fragment. Deviation from the sibling convention: unlike jtmm-catalogue.html (a full head with plan-slug/reckon-type meta) and jtmm-coil-element-names.html (a meta paragraph naming node, date and plan section), this fragment carries no meta line at all - it opens directly with the section element and names the plan and section 6 only in prose. It remains self-identifying through its section id and the dispatch node name in the scope paragraph, so the deviation is stylistic and does not defeat composition. No version tag, sprint or ticket identifier appears in the body; the section-number references are the plan's own numbering.
justifications.goal_fidelity: The section-6 dispatch asks jtmm-jt60sa-host-survey to (a) discover the site's other hosts from passive sources only, (b) record per host what the sources say it serves, (c) record whether the name resolves and whether a port named in site configuration accepts a TCP connection from each server, (d) look for where FAME's records went (migrated stores, archived dumps, copies of FAME3, any archive carrying psi and q), and (e) attempt one OP1 slice read for each source it finds. The fragment answers (a) with an 85-name host registry read from the EQDB client's own endian_info table, verbatim, plus /etc/fstab, /proc/mounts, /etc/resolv.conf and the *.eqdbms endpoint config; (b) with a per-host row naming the source and what it serves; (c) by reporting the resolution measure for each host and stating plainly that no port is named in the site configuration read, so that measure has no subject rather than being silently dropped; (d) by testing every FAME store path the configuration names (/JT60SA_EQ/FAME3, /analysis_DB/FAME3, /dbhome/h060028/FAME3) and finding none present, with the parent /analysis_DB listed as holding only EDASDB and MBDB; and (e) with one OP1 slice read (E101011 G-EQDSK psi (129,129), q (129,)). nakasvr23 is disclosed as unreachable (kex_exchange_identification) and no claim is made for nakasvr23 anywhere in the fragment. Deduction: two of the dispatch's measures are left unresolved - the cloud is one-server, and the port measure has no subject - but both are disclosed as the run's own follow-ons rather than presented as completed. The goal of a passive-source survey with a FAME-record search over the reachable server is met; the nakasvr23 half is unmet for an external reason the run names and evidences.
justifications.reuse: The node reused the site's own tools rather than re-deriving anything: the host registry is the EQDB client's own endian_info table, the resolver is the platform's getent hosts, and the one slice read uses the reader /home/d240034/prova/eqdsk.py (eqdsk_read) on the site's own EFIT95.DATA rather than writing a G-EQDSK parser. It adds no library code and changes no product source and no test; its only artifacts are the fragment and the small read-only collection scripts. Deduction: the seven collection scripts are one-shot helpers that a shared survey harness could parameterise, but they are not duplication the node could have avoided within a single-node read-only survey, and no existing shared helper covers this task.
justifications.scope_discipline: git show --stat 63416167 and git diff --stat 2e3e3f68..54368aaf both list exactly one file, docs/evidence/fragments/jt60sa-machine-map/jtmm-jt60sa-host-survey.html, 212 insertions, which is the manifest's declared changed_path and within the node's declared write scope (the fragment and the figures directory). No product source and no test is touched. The run's read scope matches the dispatch: I read all seven collection scripts (collect_a..f.sh) and every one is read-only - /etc configuration, /analysis and /analysis_DB, /work, and the lead-named /home/d240034; none reads keys, credentials, shell history or any other user's home, and none writes outside the repository. No port scan or ping sweep appears in any batch. The seven batches are exactly the seven collection batches the second commit corrects the fragment to name (commit 54368aaf fixes 'five' to 'seven').
